title: What's New in Inference Engineering — Philip Kiely, Baseten
talk_summary: The talk surveys data-center inference optimizations: quantization (TurboQuant), KV-cache compaction, speculative decoding (DFlash), and continuous speculator retraining. Most are serving-stack techniques, but the caching, compression, and draft-verify mechanisms have analogies for agent context and model routing.

takeaways.what_they_do: They reuse prefill KV cache when the prompt prefix matches, so stable prefixes avoid recomputation.
takeaways.evidence_quote: If you put in the same prompt with the same prefix, uh you get to reuse the tokens that you calculated prefill on last time.

takeaways.what_they_do: They discuss compressing remembered context as a middle ground between full context and RAG/files, aiming for high compression with near-lossless retention.
takeaways.evidence_quote: quite a bit of compression in the data that you remembering with near lossless information retention

takeaways.technique: Reject memory-saving modes that halve throughput
takeaways.what_they_do: TurboQuant halves KV-cache memory but adds forward-pass compute and cuts TPS by more than half, so they reject it for production.
takeaways.evidence_quote: it cuts TPS by more than half and that's just an unacceptable trade-off
takeaways.numbers: 4-bit vs 8-bit KV cache; TPS cut by more than half

takeaways.what_they_do: Speculative decoding uses draft tokens verified by the target model, making the speedup lossless when verification passes.
takeaways.evidence_quote: we're going to use draft tokens. We're going to verify them during the forward pass

takeaways.what_they_do: They note speculative decoding depends on actual prompt/response distribution and continuous retraining on live traffic improves acceptance.
takeaways.evidence_quote: speculative decoding is very dependent on the actual content of the prompts and responses
takeaways.numbers: 20% to even 2x improvement in token acceptance rates
